Short questions to test your understanding of continuous-time Markov chains. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Throughout we use **row vectors** and the convention **row = from, column = to**. Off the diagonal, $q_{ij}$ is the rate from $i$ to $j$; the diagonal is $q_{ii} = -q_i$, minus the total leaving rate, so **rows of $Q$ sum to 0**.

---

**Q1.** What is the difference between the number $0.3$ on an arrow of a discrete-time chain and the number $0.3$ /min on an arrow of a continuous-time chain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One is a probability, the other has units.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In discrete time, $0.3$ is the **probability** of taking that arrow in one step. In continuous time, $0.3$ /min is a **rate**: the expected number of such jumps per minute while in that state. A rate has units and can be larger than 1. Only for a short time $\Delta t$ does it turn into a probability, about $0.3\,\Delta t$.
:::

---

**Q2.** An ion channel closes at rate $5$ per millisecond while it is open. How long does it stay open on average? What kind of distribution do the open times follow?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Waiting time with total leaving rate $q$: which distribution, and what is its mean?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The open time is **exponential** with rate 5 per ms, so the mean open time is $1/5 = 0.2$ ms. Most openings are shorter than that, a few are much longer.
:::

---

**Q3.** A cell in state prog can go to stem at rate $0.1$ per day or to diff at rate $0.3$ per day. What is its total leaving rate, its mean time in prog, and the probability that its next jump is to diff?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Add the rates for "when"; divide for "where".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Total leaving rate $q = 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4$ per day, so the mean time in prog is $1/0.4 = 2.5$ days. The next jump goes to diff with probability $0.3/0.4 = 0.75$.
:::

---

**Q4.** Write the rate matrix $Q$ for the chain in Q3 if, in addition, stem → prog at rate $0.2$ and diff → prog at rate $0.05$ per day (states ordered stem, prog, diff; no other arrows). Check the rows.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Fill in the off-diagonals from the arrows, then make each diagonal entry minus the rest of its row.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -0.2 & 0.2 & 0\\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.3\\ 0 & 0.05 & -0.05 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Rows: $-0.2 + 0.2 + 0 = 0$, $0.1 - 0.4 + 0.3 = 0$, $0 + 0.05 - 0.05 = 0$. ✓
:::

---

**Q5.** Is $\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ a valid rate matrix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Check the row sums.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Row 1 sums to $-1 + 0.5 = -0.5 \ne 0$. (Row 2 is fine.) The diagonal must be exactly minus the sum of the other rates in its row.
:::

---

**Q6.** A gene promoter switches ON → OFF at rate $a = 2$ per hour and OFF → ON at rate $b = 0.5$ per hour. What fraction of the time is it ON in the long run? Use flow balance.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Flow ON→OFF is $\pi_{\text{ON}}\,a$; flow OFF→ON is $\pi_{\text{OFF}}\,b$. Set them equal and use $\pi_{\text{ON}} + \pi_{\text{OFF}} = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2\,\pi_{\text{ON}} = 0.5\,\pi_{\text{OFF}}$, so $\pi_{\text{OFF}} = 4\,\pi_{\text{ON}}$ and $\pi_{\text{ON}} = 1/5 = 0.2$. Equivalently $b/(a+b) = 0.5/2.5 = 0.2$, or from the mean times: ON lasts $1/2 = 0.5$ h, OFF lasts $1/0.5 = 2$ h, and $0.5/(0.5 + 2) = 0.2$.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two promoters have rates $(a, b) = (2, 1)$ and $(0.2, 0.1)$ per minute. Do they have the same stationary distribution? Which one reaches it faster, and by how much?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For 2 states, $\boldsymbol\pi$ depends on the ratio of the rates; the approach to $\boldsymbol\pi$ goes like $e^{-(a+b)t}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same $\boldsymbol\pi = (b, a)/(a+b) = (1/3, 2/3)$ for both, because the ratio $a : b$ is the same. The first relaxes with rate $a + b = 3$ per min, the second with $0.3$ per min, so the first approaches $\boldsymbol\pi$ **10 times faster**.
:::

---

**Q8.** For the promoter in Q6, write $P \approx I + Q\,\Delta t$ for $\Delta t = 0.1$ hour. Why must $\Delta t$ be small?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2\\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. Multiply by $\Delta t$ and add the identity. What happens to the diagonal when $\Delta t$ is large?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1 - 0.2 & 0.2\\ 0.05 & 1 - 0.05 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2\\ 0.05 & 0.95 \end{pmatrix}$; rows sum to 1. The approximation uses "probability ≈ rate × time", which is only accurate when rate × time is small. For large $\Delta t$ (here above $0.5$ h) the diagonal entry $1 - 2\Delta t$ even becomes negative, which no probability can be.
:::

---

**Q9.** True or false: in a continuous-time chain, a state with no arrows out is absorbing, and its row of $Q$ is all zeros.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the total leaving rate of such a state, and what does that make the diagonal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
True. Its total leaving rate is 0, so the diagonal is $-0 = 0$ and the whole row is 0. The waiting time $\text{Exp}(0)$ is infinite: once there, a walker never leaves.
:::
